A real neuron is a complicated thing, but a surprising amount of its behaviour
can be captured by treating it as a leaky bucket. Current flows in, the
membrane voltage rises, some of it leaks away, and once the voltage reaches a
threshold the neuron fires a spike and starts over. That is the leaky
integrate-and-fire model. It goes back to Lapicque (1907), long before anyone
knew what an action potential was made of, and it is still the first model
most people meet in computational neuroscience. I used it in a webinar for the German Neuroscience
Olympiad in 2020, and this page is the interactive version of that notebook.

Everything runs in your browser. The simulation keeps going while you move the
sliders, so you can watch the neuron react to a change in its input.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// shared helpers: one persistent canvas per explorable, text-sized fonts, responsive width
exFont = ({size: getComputedStyle(document.body).fontSize, family: getComputedStyle(document.body).fontFamily, toString() { return this.size + " " + this.family; }})
exFg = () => getComputedStyle(document.body).color
mkCanvas = (W, H) => {
  const c = DOM.context2d(W, H);
  c.canvas.style.width = "100%"; c.canvas.style.maxWidth = W + "px"; c.canvas.style.height = "auto";
  return c;
}
axisBox = (c, x, y, w, h) => { c.strokeStyle = "#999"; c.lineWidth = 1; c.strokeRect(x, y, w, h); }
```

## The model

The only variable is the membrane potential $V$, measured in millivolts. Left
alone, it sits at the resting potential $V_{\text{rest}} = -65$ mV. An input
current $I$ pushes it away from rest, and the leak pulls it back, so that

$$\tau_m \frac{dV}{dt} = (V_{\text{rest}} - V) + R\,I(t).$$

The membrane time constant $\tau_m$ sets how fast $V$ follows a change in
input. A small $\tau_m$ means a nervous neuron that tracks its input closely,
a large one means a sluggish neuron that averages over a longer stretch of
time. The input resistance $R$ converts current to voltage and is fixed at
2 MΩ here, so a steady current of 10 nA lifts the voltage by 20 mV in the long
run.

The equation alone would just let $V$ settle at a new level. The spike is
added by hand: whenever $V$ reaches the threshold $V_{\text{th}}$, the neuron
is said to fire, $V$ is reset to $V_{\text{reset}} = -70$ mV, and it is held
there for a refractory period of 2 ms before the integration starts again.
Nothing about the shape of a real action potential is in the model. The spike
is just an event, drawn here as a vertical stroke so that you can see it.

With noise switched on, a random Gaussian value is added to the current at
every time step. The slider sets the size of these fluctuations. This is a
crude stand-in for the thousands of synaptic inputs a cortical neuron
receives, which never add up to a perfectly steady current.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof lifI = Inputs.range([0, 25], {value: 8, step: 0.5, label: "Input current (nA)"})
viewof lifNoise = Inputs.range([0, 10], {value: 0, step: 0.5, label: "Input noise (0 = off)"})
viewof lifTau = Inputs.range([2, 50], {value: 10, step: 1, label: "Membrane time constant τ (ms)"})
viewof lifThr = Inputs.range([-60, -35], {value: -50, step: 1, label: "Threshold (mV)"})
viewof lifPause = Inputs.toggle({label: "Pause"})
viewof lifReset = Inputs.button("Reset (also clears the f-I points)")
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
lifState = {
  lifReset;
  const dt = 0.1, win = 300, R = 2, Vrest = -65, Vreset = -70, refr = 2;
  const n = Math.round(win / dt);
  const V = new Float32Array(n).fill(Vrest), Iarr = new Float32Array(n);
  let v = Vrest, refrLeft = 0, t = 0;
  const fi = new Map();
  let key = null, sinceChange = 0, spikesSince = 0, lastSig = 0;
  const gauss = () => { let u = 0; while (u === 0) u = Math.random();
                        return Math.sqrt(-2 * Math.log(u)) * Math.cos(2 * Math.PI * Math.random()); };
  while (true) {
    const I0 = viewof lifI.value, sig = viewof lifNoise.value,
          tau = viewof lifTau.value, thr = viewof lifThr.value;
    if (!viewof lifPause.value) {
      const k = `${I0}|${sig > 0}`;
      if (sig > 0 && sig !== lastSig) { for (const [kk, p] of fi) if (p.noisy) fi.delete(kk); }
      if (sig > 0) lastSig = sig;
      if (k !== key) { key = k; sinceChange = 0; spikesSince = 0; }
      for (let s = 0; s < 20; s++) {
        const I = I0 + sig * gauss() / Math.sqrt(dt);
        if (refrLeft > 0) { refrLeft -= dt; v = Vreset; }
        else {
          v += dt / tau * ((Vrest - v) + R * I);
          if (v >= thr) { v = 20; spikesSince++; refrLeft = refr; }
        }
        V.copyWithin(0, 1); V[n - 1] = v;
        Iarr.copyWithin(0, 1); Iarr[n - 1] = I;
        if (v === 20) v = Vreset;
        t += dt; sinceChange += dt;
      }
      if (sinceChange >= 500) fi.set(key, {I: I0, noisy: sig > 0, rate: 1000 * spikesSince / sinceChange});
    }
    yield {V, Iarr, t, win, fi, thr, tau, sig, I0, R, Vrest, refr,
           rate: sinceChange > 0 ? 1000 * spikesSince / sinceChange : 0};
  }
}
lifCanvas = mkCanvas(760, 360)
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const {V, Iarr, win, fi, thr, tau, sig, I0, R, Vrest, refr, rate} = lifState;
  const blue = "#1f77b4", orange = "#ff7f0e", c = lifCanvas, fg = exFg();
  const W = 760, H = 360, n = V.length;
  c.clearRect(0, 0, W, H); c.font = exFont;
  // traces, left
  const mL = 80, trR = 470;
  const top = {y0: 12, h: 80, lo: -10, hi: 35};
  const bot = {y0: 112, h: 200, lo: -80, hi: 30};
  const sx = i => mL + (trR - mL) * i / (n - 1);
  const sy = (p, v) => p.y0 + p.h * (1 - (v - p.lo) / (p.hi - p.lo));
  for (const p of [top, bot]) axisBox(c, mL, p.y0, trR - mL, p.h);
  c.fillStyle = fg; c.textAlign = "right";
  c.fillText("I (nA)", mL - 8, top.y0 + top.h / 2 + 5);
  c.fillText("V (mV)", mL - 8, bot.y0 + bot.h / 2 + 5);
  c.fillText(thr, mL - 8, sy(bot, thr) + 5); c.fillText("-65", mL - 8, sy(bot, -65) + 5);
  c.textAlign = "center"; c.fillText(`last ${win} ms`, (mL + trR) / 2, H - 14);
  c.textAlign = "right"; c.fillText(`${rate.toFixed(0)} spikes / s`, trR - 8, bot.y0 + 20);
  c.setLineDash([4, 4]); c.strokeStyle = "red"; c.beginPath(); c.moveTo(mL, sy(bot, thr)); c.lineTo(trR, sy(bot, thr)); c.stroke(); c.setLineDash([]);
  c.strokeStyle = "#888"; c.lineWidth = 1; c.beginPath();
  for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) { const y = sy(top, Math.max(top.lo, Math.min(top.hi, Iarr[i]))); i ? c.lineTo(sx(i), y) : c.moveTo(sx(0), y); }
  c.stroke();
  c.strokeStyle = sig > 0 ? orange : blue; c.lineWidth = 1.5; c.beginPath();
  for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) i ? c.lineTo(sx(i), sy(bot, V[i])) : c.moveTo(sx(0), sy(bot, V[0]));
  c.stroke();
  // f-I curve, right
  const fP = {x0: 560, y0: 12, w: 180, h: 300};
  const Imax = 25, fmax = Math.max(100, ...Array.from(fi.values()).map(p => p.rate)) * 1.1;
  const fx = I => fP.x0 + fP.w * I / Imax, fy = f => fP.y0 + fP.h * (1 - f / fmax);
  axisBox(c, fP.x0, fP.y0, fP.w, fP.h);
  c.fillStyle = fg; c.textAlign = "center";
  c.fillText("input (nA)", fP.x0 + fP.w / 2, H - 14);
  c.fillText("0", fx(0), fP.y0 + fP.h + 20); c.fillText(Imax, fx(Imax), fP.y0 + fP.h + 20);
  c.save(); c.translate(fP.x0 - 44, fP.y0 + fP.h / 2); c.rotate(-Math.PI / 2); c.fillText("spikes / s", 0, 0); c.restore();
  c.textAlign = "right"; c.fillText("0", fP.x0 - 6, fy(0) + 5); c.fillText(fmax.toFixed(0), fP.x0 - 6, fy(fmax) + 5);
  c.setLineDash([3, 3]); c.strokeStyle = blue; c.lineWidth = 1; c.beginPath(); let started = false;
  for (let I = 0; I <= Imax; I += 0.1) {
    const d = R * I - (thr - Vrest); if (d <= 0) continue;
    const f = Math.min(fmax, 1000 / (refr + tau * Math.log(R * I / d)));
    started ? c.lineTo(fx(I), fy(f)) : c.moveTo(fx(I), fy(f)); started = true;
  }
  c.stroke(); c.setLineDash([]);
  for (const [k, p] of fi) { c.fillStyle = p.noisy ? orange : blue; c.beginPath(); c.arc(fx(p.I), fy(p.rate), 5, 0, 2 * Math.PI); c.fill(); }
  c.strokeStyle = sig > 0 ? orange : blue; c.lineWidth = 2; c.beginPath(); c.arc(fx(I0), fy(Math.min(rate, fmax)), 8, 0, 2 * Math.PI); c.stroke();
  c.textAlign = "left"; c.fillStyle = blue; c.fillText("noise-free", fP.x0 + 8, fP.y0 + 22);
  c.fillStyle = orange; c.fillText(sig > 0 ? `noise ${sig}` : "noise (off)", fP.x0 + 8, fP.y0 + 44);
  return c.canvas;
}
```

## Reading the figure

The two panels on the left show the last 300 ms of the simulation. The upper
one is the input current, the lower one the membrane potential, blue while the
input is noise-free and orange once you add noise. The red dashed line is the
threshold. Each time the trace touches it you see a spike drawn up to +20 mV,
then the voltage drops to the reset value and climbs again. The number in the
corner is the firing rate, averaged since you last changed a setting.

The panel on the right is the f-I curve, the firing rate as a function of the
input current. This is the standard way to characterise a neuron, and the
page builds it up from your own experiments: every input strength you leave
the neuron at for half a second adds a dot. Blue dots are noise-free
measurements, orange dots were taken at the current noise level. Changing the
noise level clears the orange dots, because they no longer belong to the same
curve. The open ring shows where the current setting sits.

The blue dashed line is not a measurement. It is the exact firing rate of the
noise-free model, which you can work out by hand: the time the voltage needs
to climb from reset to threshold under a constant current, plus the
refractory period, is one interspike interval, and the rate is its inverse,

$$f = \frac{1}{t_{\text{ref}} + \tau_m \ln \dfrac{RI}{RI - (V_{\text{th}} - V_{\text{rest}})}} .$$

The formula makes two things obvious. Below the rheobase current
$I = (V_{\text{th}} - V_{\text{rest}})/R$, the voltage never reaches threshold
and the rate is zero, so the curve has a hard corner. And at large currents
the rate saturates at $1/t_{\text{ref}}$, because the neuron cannot fire
faster than once per refractory period.

## Things to try

Start with the noise off and raise the current slowly. Nothing happens until
you cross 7.5 nA, and then the neuron starts firing at a rate that goes up
quickly at first and then more slowly. Your dots should land on the dashed
curve.

Now set the current to 6 nA, just below the rheobase, and turn on the noise.
The voltage hovers below threshold and crosses it now and then, so the neuron
fires at a low and irregular rate where the noise-free model is silent. Take
a few measurements at different currents and compare the orange dots with the
dashed line. Noise does not just add scatter, it rounds off the corner of the
f-I curve, and this smoothing is the main reason real neurons do not show a
hard threshold in their rate.

Change the time constant. With a long $\tau_m$ the voltage trace is smooth
and the neuron is slow to respond, but the noise-free f-I curve shifts too,
since a slower climb means a longer interval. With a short $\tau_m$ and noise
on, the trace becomes jagged and the firing increasingly random.

The model and the f-I formula are treated in Dayan and Abbott (2001, chapter
5) and at greater length in Gerstner et al. (2014), which also covers what
noise does to the firing statistics. Brunel and van Rossum (2007) tell the
story of Lapicque's original paper.
